<output> Imagine that now I want to compute, without knowing anything about density operators, what happens if I measure an observable $O$, and I measure it many times, and at the end, I compute the expectation value of this observable.
We can do it very simply using classical statistics. The expectation value of $O$ would be, in the limit of an infinite number of measurements, the sum over all possible outcomes $o_i$ of the probability of obtaining that outcome times its value: $\langle O \rangle = \sum_i P(o_i) o_i$.
Now, the probability $P(o_i)$ of obtaining outcome $o_i$ can be written using conditional probabilities as $P(o_i) = \sum_j P(\psi_j) P(o_i | \psi_j)$, where $P(\psi_j)$ is the probability of having state $\ket{\psi_j}$ in the box, and $P(o_i | \psi_j)$ is the probability of obtaining outcome $o_i$ given that the state was $\ket{\psi_j}$. This is just the law of total probability that you have seen in classical statistics.
And the conditional probability $P(o_i | \psi_j)$ is given, according to the measurement postulate, by $P(o_i | \psi_j) = \bra{\psi_j} P_i \ket{\psi_j}$, where $P_i$ is the projector onto the eigenspace of $O$ with eigenvalue $o_i$.
So the expectation value is $$ \langle O \rangle = \sum_i \sum_j P(\psi_j) \bra{\psi_j} P_i \ket{\psi_j} o_i $$ But now look at what happens. We can rewrite this as $$ \langle O \rangle = \sum_i \tr\left(\sum_j P(\psi_j) \ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j} P_i\right) o_i $$ using the linearity and cyclic property of the trace. And now we can write $$ \langle O \rangle = \tr\left(\sum_i \sum_j P(\psi_j) \ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j} P_i o_i\right) = \tr(\rho O) $$ where $\rho = \sum_j P(\psi_j) \ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j}$ is exactly the density operator as we defined it.
So, in other words, you could have just taken the classical probabilities and the measurement postulate and computed everything using the laws of probability theory. And at the end, what you get is the same result as if you had first computed the density operator and then used the formula $\langle O \rangle = \tr(\rho O)$. </output> </example> </examples>
